newsitem.title: ZAIRE: No joy in Zaire capital as Mobutu hangs on.
newsitem.headline: No joy in Zaire capital as Mobutu hangs on.

text.p: Inconclusive talks on ending Zaire's civil war have left many in the capital Kinshasa feeling frustrated. Some say President Mobutu Sese Seko spoilt the party by refusing to step down from power, others fear what might happen next.

But with rebel leader Laurent Kabila refusing to declare a truce and his rebels advancing down the road to Kinshasa, markets operated normally and there was no sign of new military checkpoints in the centre of the city of five million people.
"Mobutu should have stayed away for good," said newspaper vendor Paul Mbwaza, clutching several Kinshasa dailies sporting banner headlines on the talks aboard a South African ship.
"Champagne had been chilled to celebrate the departure of the leopard," commented the opposition daily Le Potentiel, referring to Mobutu, who always sports a leopard skin cap.
"But Mobutu spoilt the party by presenting a three-point plan, throwing the (capital) city into uncertainty," it said.
Mobutu's movements were not immediately clear.
Witnesses at Ndjili international airport, 25 km (16 miles) from the capital and in the advancing rebels' path, reported that Mobutu's plane had returned.

Emergency rule Prime Minister Likulia Bolongo met the plane but public access was restricted and although a motorcade with smoked glass windows was seen leaving the airport no one actually saw the veteran president.
Political commentator Tshidibi Ngodavi, writing in Le Potentiel, likened Mobutu to a "a tired leopard, around whom antelopes, sheep, goats and all sorts of animals move freely without any fear."
But despite the veneer of calm, many in the capital betrayed anxiety that war would inevitably come to the city.

The independent daily La Reference Plus said Mobutu's decision to hang on could trigger a rebel assault on the city. "The carnage that everyone has been fearing for days would very much be the order of the day," it said.
There were no signs of stepped up military activity in the capital on Monday even though many newspapers carried reports of rebel claims of being within 60 km (35 miles) of the city.
But on the road east to Kenge, the nearest town to Kinshasa taken by rebels, witnesses saw special presidential guard units manning a bridge about 30 km (18 miles) from the capital.
A flatbed military truck carrying a multiple rocket launcher raced by heading in the direction of Kenge, followed by another loaded with ammunition and supplies.
A DSP soldier among a group of 30 told reporters: "We're going to stop Kabila. He's not coming here."
Kabila's forces say their immediate target is Kinshasa airport but international airlines have not cancelled flights.

Officials at South Africa Airways, the Belgian carrier Sabena and Ethiopian Airlines all said they were maintaining their services. A Sabena flight arrived on schedule on Monday morning and was due to return to Brussels later.
Asked about the rebels, a Sabena official said: "They're still far away."

There was no sign of a rush by Kinshasa residents to flee to Congo's capital Brazzaville across River Zaire, partly because of a decree by Kinshasa's military governor last week requiring exit visas for the crossing.
Most Kinshasa residents say openly they would welcome the rebels and that their only fear is the reaction of the army.
To date, unpaid and demoralised troops have spent more time looting than fighting the rebels.
